doc: Distance between the commissures of the mouth more than 2 SD below the mean. Alternatively, an apparently decreased width of the oral aperture (subjective).
Posterior displacement of the tongue into the pharynx, i.e., a tongue that is mislocalised posteriorly.

A type of abnormal location of the ears in which the position of the ears is characterized by posterior rotation (the superior part of the ears is rotated towards the back of the head, and the inferior part of the ears towards the front).

Dental malocclusion refers to an abnormality of the occlusion, or alignment, of the teeth and the way the upper and lower teeth fit together, resulting in overcrowding of teeth or in abnormal bite patterns.
Cleft between the helix and the lobe.
Decreased length and width of the tongue.
A decreased magnitude of the sensory perception of sound.

A height below that which is expected according to age and gender norms. Although there is no universally accepted definition of short stature, many refer to "short stature" as height more than 2 standard deviations below the mean for age and gender (or below the 3rd percentile for age and gender dependent norms).

Anteriorly-facing nostrils viewed with the head in the Frankfurt horizontal and the eyes of the observer level with the eyes of the subject. This gives the appearance of an upturned nose (upturned nasal tip).
An abnormal restriction of fetal growth with fetal weight below the tenth percentile for gestational age.

A measured foot length that is more than 2 SD below the mean for a newborn of 27 - 41 weeks gestation, or foot that is less than the 3rd centile for individuals from birth to 16 years of age (objective). Alternatively, a foot that appears disproportionately short (subjective).
One or more abnormally short long bone.

A short femur length is defined as either a measurement below the 2.5th percentile for gestational age or a measurement that is less than 0.9 of that predicted by the measured biparietal diameter. The femur should be measured with the bone perpendicular to the ultrasound beam and with epiphyseal cartilages visible but not included in the measurement (PMID:16100637).

Cone-shaped epiphyses of the phalanges of the hands or feet. Cone-shaped epiphyses (also known as coned epiphyses) are epiphyses that invaginate into cupped metaphyses. That is, the epiphysis has a cone-shaped distal extension resulting from increased growth of the central portion of the epiphysis relative to its periphery.
The presence of a stenosis (narrowing) of the aortic valve.
An abnormality of the mitral valve characterized by insufficiency or incompetence of the mitral valve resulting in retrograde leaking of blood through the mitral valve upon ventricular contraction.
Abnormally increased size of the liver.
An abnormal gait pattern characterized by the failure of the heel to contact the floor at the onset of stance during gait.
Failure of the immune system to protect the body adequately from infection, due to the absence or insufficiency of some component process or substance.
An abnormally decreased level of immunoglobulin in blood.
Inflammation of the conjunctiva.
A developmental anomaly characterized by abnormal smallness of one or both eyes.

A congenital brain malformation typically characterized by incomplete formation of the cerebellar vermis, dilation of the fourth ventricle, and enlargement of the posterior fossa. In layman's terms, Dandy Walker malformation is a cyst in the cerebellum (typically symmetrical) that is involved with the fourth ventricle. This may interfere with the ability to drain cerebrospinal fluid from the brain, resulting in hydrocephalus. Dandy Walker cysts are formed during early embryonic development, while the brain forms. The cyst in the cerebellum typically has several blood vessels running through it connecting to the brain, thereby prohibiting surgical removal.
Any abnormality of the eye, including location, spacing, and intraocular abnormalities.
Interalar distance more than two standard deviations above the mean for age, i.e., an apparently increased width of the nasal base and alae.

An abnormality of the skull, the bony framework of the head which is comprised of the neurocranium (with eight cranial bones) and the viscerocranium (facial skeleton) that comprises fourteen facial bones with the mandible as its largest bone.
An abnormality of the pigmentation of the skin.

A seizure is an intermittent abnormality of nervous system physiology characterized by a transient occurrence of signs and/or symptoms due to abnormal excessive or synchronous neuronal activity in the brain.

Hypotonia is an abnormally low muscle tone (the amount of tension or resistance to movement in a muscle). Even when relaxed, muscles have a continuous and passive partial contraction which provides some resistance to passive stretching. Hypotonia thus manifests as diminished resistance to passive stretching. Hypotonia is not the same as muscle weakness, although the two conditions can co-exist.
A developmental defect in the formation of pulmonary lobes.
An organ or organ-system abnormality that consists of uncontrolled autonomous cell-proliferation which can occur in any part of the body as a benign or malignant neoplasm (tumor).
Osteolysis refers to the destruction of bone through bone resorption with removal or loss of calcium.
An abnormality of the arm.
Clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorders characterized by dysplasia (ineffective production) in one or more hematopoietic cell lineages, leading to anemia and cytopenia.
The presence of six or more cafe-au-lait spots.
A functional abnormality of the immune system.
A tumor (abnormal growth of tissue) of the vagina.
The presence of multiple polyps in the intestine.
An abnormality of the skin characterized the presence of excessive amounts of dry surface scales on the skin resulting from an abnormality of keratinization.
Increased width of the skin of vermilion border region of upper lip.
A structural anomaly of the nervous system.
Limitation in the ability to open the mouth.
An abnormality of the philtrum.

A spectrum of malformations of cortical development caused by insufficient neuronal migration that subsumes the terms agyria, pachygyria and subcortical band heterotopia. See also neuropathological definitions for 2-, 3-, and 4-layered lissencephaly.
A foot for which the measured width is above the 95th centile for age; or, a foot that appears disproportionately wide for its length.
An anomaly of the vermis of cerebellum.
Sudden and involuntary contractions of one or more muscles.
Increased convexity of the occiput (posterior part of the skull).

Osteopenia is a term to define bone density that is not normal but also not as low as osteoporosis. By definition from the World Health Organization osteopenia is defined by bone densitometry as a T score -1 to -2.5.
Increased volume and globular shape of the anteroinferior aspect of the nose.
Absence of a fingernail.
Generalized excessive, abnormal hairiness.
Increased thickness of the external ear.
An increase in height of the medial longitudinal arch of the foot that does not flatten on weight bearing (i.e., a distinctly hollow form of the sole of the foot when it is bearing weight).
The presence of one or more teeth additional to the normal number.

Continuous involuntary sustained muscle contraction. When an affected muscle is passively stretched, the degree of resistance remains constant regardless of the rate at which the muscle is stretched. This feature helps to distinguish rigidity from muscle spasticity.

A type of ataxia characterized by the impairment of the ability to perform rapidly alternating movements, such as pronating and supinating his or her hand on the dorsum of the other hand as rapidly as possible.
Any abnormality of the palate, i.e., of roof of the mouth.

Any abnormality of the skeletal muscle cell. Muscle fibers are subdivided into two types. Type I fibers are fatigue-resistant and rich in oxidative enzymes (they stain light with the myosin ATPase reaction), and type II fibers are fast-contracting, fatigue-prone, and rich in glycolytic enzymes (these fibers stain darkly). Normal muscle tissue has a random distribution of type I and type II fibers.
Involuntary contractions of the neck musculature resulting in an abnormal posture of or abnormal movements of the head.
Reduced strength of muscles.
Displacement of the femur from its normal location in the hip joint.
An outward deviation of the foot at the talocalcaneal or subtalar joint.
Distention of the abdomen.
The presence of many cysts in the kidney.
The condition of being unable to eat a full meal because of a feeling of fullness (satiety), or or feeling very full after eating only a small amount of food.
Increased level of the enzyme gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT). GGT is mainly present in kidney, liver, and pancreatic cells, but small amounts are present in other tissues.

Visual impairment (or vision impairment) is vision loss (of a person) to such a degree as to qualify as an additional support need through a significant limitation of visual capability resulting from either disease, trauma, or congenital or degenerative conditions that cannot be corrected by conventional means, such as refractive correction, medication, or surgery.
Any abnormality of the electrical responses of various cell types in the retina as measured by electroretinography.
Obstruction of the flow of urine through the urethra.
Infrequent or difficult evacuation of feces.

Fasciculations are observed as small, local, involuntary muscle contractions (twitching) visible under the skin. Fasciculations result from increased irritability of an axon (which in turn is often a manifestation of disease of a motor neuron). This leads to sporadic discharges of all the muscle fibers controlled by the axon in isolation from other motor units.
An acquired language impairment of some or all of the abilities to produce or comprehend speech and to read or write.
Any structural anomaly that affects the motor neuron.

A functional anomaly of the upper motor neuron. The upper motor neurons are neurons of the primary motor cortex which project to the brainstem and spinal chord via the corticonuclear, corticobulbar and corticospinal (pyramidal) tracts. They are involved in control of voluntary movements. Dysfunction leads to weakness, impairment of fine motor movements, spasticity, hyperreflexia and abnormal pyramidal signs.

Reduced function of the muscles required to generate subatmospheric pressure in the thoracic cavity during breathing: the diaphragm, the external intercostal and the interchondral part of the internal intercostal muscles.

An increased sensitivity of the skin to light. Photosensitivity may result in a rash upon exposure to the sun (which is known as photodermatosis). Photosensitivity can be diagnosed by phototests in which light is shone on small areas of skin.
A hyperpigmented circumscribed area of change in normal skin color without elevation or depression of any size.
The presence of an increased number of freckles, small circular spots on the skin that are darker than the surrounding skin because of deposits of melanin.
The presence of a fistula (abnormal tunnel) between the anal canal and the perineum.
An abnormal increase in the number of leukocytes in the blood.
A sudden sensation of feeling cold.

Tumor-like growths that consist of replacement of the medullary bone with fibrous tissue, causing the expansion and weakening of the areas of bone involved. Especially when involving the skull or facial bones, the lesions can cause externally visible deformities. The skull is often, but not necessarily, affected, and any other bone or bones may be involved. Fibrous dysplasia can either effect isolated bones (Monostotic fibrous dysplasia) or also generalized all bones of the body (Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia).
Any anomaly in the composite material or the layered arrangement of the bony skeleton.

To avoid pain weight is put on the affected leg for as short a time as possible, resulting in a limp. The patients appear to be walking as if there were a thorn in the sole of the foot. To reduce the load on the affected leg the patients lift and lower their foot in a fixed ankle position.
Any abnormality of the clavicles (collar bones).
Any abnormality of the parietal bone of the skull.
Irregular distribution of the teeth along the dental arch, i.e., and irregular spatial pattern of teeth.

A malignant bone tumor that usually develops during adolescence and usually affects the long bones including the tibia, femur, and humerus. The typical symptoms of osteosarcoma comprise bone pain, fracture, limitation of motion, and tenderness or swelling at the site of the tumor.

Overproduction of the hormone of cortisol by the adrenal cortex, resulting in a characteristic combination of clinical symptoms termed Cushing syndrome, with truncal obesity, a round, full face, striae atrophicae and acne, muscle weakness, and other features.
A disorder of muscle unrelated to impairment of innervation or neuromuscular junction.
Abnormal results of investigations using electromyography (EMG).
Applies to a disease manifestation that increases in scope or severity over the course of time, i.e., that worsens with age.
A generalized disorder of peripheral nerves.
Facial diplegia refers to bilateral facial palsy (bilateral facial palsy is much rarer than unilateral facial palsy).
Demyelinating neuropathy is characterized by slow nerve conduction velocities with reduced amplitudes of sensory/motor nerve conduction and prolonged distal latencies.

Repeated episodes of segmental demyelination and remyelination lead to the accumulation of supernumerary Schwann cells around axons, which is referred to as onion bulb formation. This finding affects peripheral nerves.
Increased concentration of protein in the cerebrospinal fluid.
Rhythmic, involuntary oscillations of one or both eyes related to abnormality in fixation, conjugate gaze, or vestibular mechanisms.

Craniosynostosis refers to the premature closure of the cranial sutures. Primary craniosynostosis refers to the closure of one or more sutures due to abnormalities in skull development, and secondary craniosynostosis results from failure of brain growth.
A sudden episode of intense fear in a situation where there is no danger or apparent cause.
A conduction block of the left branch of the bundle of His. This manifests as a generalized disturbance of QRS morphology on EKG.

A mode of inheritance that is observed for traits related to a gene encoded on one of the autosomes (i.e., the human chromosomes 1-22) in which a trait manifests in heterozygotes. In the context of medical genetics, an autosomal dominant disorder is caused when a single copy of the mutant allele is present. Males and females are affected equally, and can both transmit the disorder with a risk of 50% for each child of inheriting the mutant allele.
Failure to thrive (FTT) refers to a child whose physical growth is substantially below the norm.
Overproduction of the mineralocorticoid aldosterone by the adrenal cortex.
The birth of a baby of less than 37 weeks of gestational age.
Reduction of neurologic reflexes such as the knee-jerk reaction.
Abnormally increased production of urine by the fetus resulting in polyhydramnios.

An absolute or relative decrease in retinal sensitivity extending from edge (periphery) of the visual field in a concentric pattern. The visual field is the area that is perceived simultaneously by a fixating eye.
The presence of erythrocytes that are sphere-shaped.
A type of anemia caused by premature destruction of red blood cells (hemolysis).
An abnormality of the cerebral white matter.
Sudden impairment of blood flow to a part of the brain due to occlusion or rupture of an artery to the brain.
Encephalopathy is a term that means brain disease, damage, or malfunction. In general, encephalopathy is manifested by an altered mental state.
Paralysis (complete loss of muscle function) in the arm, leg, and in some cases the face on one side of the body.

Reduced ability affecting mainly visuospatial cognition which may be tested using pattern construction (for example by Differential Ability Scales, which test a person's strengths and weaknesses across a range of intellectual abilities).

Pterygium colli is a congenital skin fold that runs along the sides of the neck down to the shoulders. It involves an ectopic fibrotic facial band superficial to the trapezius muscle. Excess hair-bearing skin is also present and extends down the cervical region well beyond the normal hairline.

Fusion of cervical vertebrae at C2 and C3, caused by a failure in the normal segmentation or division of the cervical vertebrae during the early weeks of fetal development, leading to a short neck with a low hairline at the back of the head, and restricted mobility of the upper spine.
A congenital form of torticollis resulting from shortening of the sternocleidomastoid muscle and leading to a limited range of motion in both rotation and lateral bending.
A hole between the two bottom chambers (ventricles) of the heart. The defect is centered around the most superior aspect of the ventricular septum.
Congenital absence of the anus, i.e., the opening at the bottom end of the intestinal tract.
An abnormality of the sacral bone.
A mode of inheritance that depends on genetic determinants in more than one gene.
An increase in the level of L-fucose in the urine.
The presence of a neoplasm of the urinary bladder.
Reduced strength of one or more muscles innervated by the facial nerve (the seventh cranial nerve).
A type of arrhythmia that originates above the ventricles, whereby the electrical impulse propagates down the normal His Purkinje system similar to normal sinus rhythm.
Abnormal protrusion of the scapula away from the surface of the back.
Weakness of the limb-girdle muscles (also known as the pelvic and shoulder girdles), that is, lack of strength of the muscles around the shoulders and the pelvis.
A structural abnormality of retinal vasculature.
Abnormally increased frequency (usually defined as three or more) loose or watery bowel movements a day.

A disorder of esophageal motility characterized by the inability of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax during swallowing and by inadequate or lacking peristalsis in the lower half of the body of the esophagus.

Hyperplasia of the gingiva (that is, a thickening of the soft tissue overlying the alveolar ridge. The degree of thickening ranges from involvement of the interdental papillae alone to gingival overgrowth covering the entire tooth crown.
Decreased size of the teeth, which can be defined as a mesiodistal tooth diameter (width) more than 2 SD below mean. Alternatively, an apparently decreased maximum width of tooth.
Joint stiffness is a perceived sensation of tightness in a joint or joints when attempting to move them after a period of inactivity. Joint stiffness typically subsides over time.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is defined by the presence of increased ventricular wall thickness or mass in the absence of loading conditions (hypertension, valve disease) sufficient to cause the observed abnormality.
Excessive amounts of mucopolysaccharide in the urine.
Increase in bulk of the ala nasi.
An abnormality of the structure or form of the tendons, also often called sinews.
An abnormality of the tonsils.
The presence of developmental dysplasia of the cerebral cortex.

Cortical tubers in the brain are hamartomatous lesions typically located at the gray-white matter interface, commonly in the frontal and parietal lobes. Cortical tubers are composed of abnormal glial and neural cells, and the size, number, and location vary among patients.
An abnormality of the skin that is not localized to any one particular region.
A benign tumor of cardiac striated muscle.
An abnormality of actions or reactions of a person taking place during interactions with others.
Flesh-colored papule in or around the nail bed. Ungual fibromas may be periungual (arising under the proximal nail fold) or subungual (originating under the nail plate).
A neuroendocrine tumor originating in a hormone-producing cell (islet cell) of the pancreas.
A tumor formed from the endocrine (argentaffin) cells of the mucosal lining of a variety of organs including the stomach and intestine. These cells are from neuroectodermal origin.
Infections of the skin that happen multiple times.

Metabolic acidosis (MA) is characterized by a fall in blood pH due to a reduction of serum bicarbonate concentration. This can occur as a result of either the accumulation of acids (high anion gap MA) or the loss of bicarbonate from the gastrointestinal tract or the kidney (hyperchloremic MA). By definition, MA is not due to a respirary cause.
An increased amount of creatinine in the blood.
Sepsis is defined as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection.
A resting tremor occurs when muscles are at rest and becomes less noticeable or disappears when the affected muscles are moved. Resting tremors are often slow and coarse.

Upturning of the big toe (and sometimes fanning of the other toes) in response to stimulation of the sole of the foot. If the Babinski sign is present it can indicate damage to the corticospinal tract.
An abnormality in voluntary or involuntary eye movements or their control.
Inability to initiate changes in activity or movement and to perform ordinary volitional movements rapidly and easily.
An increased lymphocyte count in the cerebrospinal fluid.
Reduction of total body weight.
Fluid accumulation in the lungs.
An abnormality of the renal tubules.

In this case the right ventricle is more muscular than normal, causing a characteristic boot-shaped (coeur-en-sabot) appearance as seen on anterior- posterior chest x-rays. Right ventricular hypertrophy is commonly associated with any form of right ventricular outflow obstruction or pulmonary hypertension, which may in turn owe its origin to left-sided disease. The echocardiographic signs are thickening of the anterior right ventricular wall and the septum. Cavity size is usually normal, or slightly enlarged. In many cases there is associated volume overload present due to tricuspid regurgitation, in the absence of this, septal motion is normal.

Pulmonary hypertension is defined mean pulmonary artery pressure of 25mmHg or more and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 15mmHg or less when measured by right heart catheterisation at rest and in a supine position.
Pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) more than 3 wood units, as defined by the current definition of pulmonary hypertension. 95% of individuals have a PVR of less than 2.4 wood units.
An unpleasant sensation characterized by physical discomfort (such as pricking, throbbing, or aching) localized to the chest.
An chronic form of hemolytic anemia.
An abnormality of the peritoneum.

Thickening of the retina that takes place due to accumulation of fluid in the macula as a nonspecific response to blood-retinal barrier breakdown. Macular edema is a common pathological response to a wide variety of ocular insults, most commonly after intraocular (e.g. cataract) surgery or in association with retinal vascular (e.g. diabetic eye disease, retinal vein occlusion) or inflammatory (e.g. uveitis) disease.

In wound repair, neovascularization (NV) involves the sprouting of new vessels from pre-existent vessels to repair or replace damaged vessels. In the retina, NV is a response to ischemia. The NV adheres to the inner surface of the retina and outer surface of the vitreous. NV are deficient in tight junctions and hence leak plasma into surrounding tissue including the vitreous. Plasma causes the vitreous gel to degenerate, contract, and eventually collapse which pulls on the retina. Since retinal NV is adherent to both retina and vitreous, as the vitreous contracts the NV may be sheared resulting in vitreous hemorrhage or the NV may remain intact and pull the retina with the vitreous resulting in retinal elevation referred to as traction retinal detachment.

A longer than normal interval (corrected for heart rate) between the Q and T waves in the heart's cycle. Prolonged QTc can cause premature action potentials during late phase depolarizations thereby leading to ventricular arrhythmias and ventricular fibrillations.

Post-exertional symptom exacerbation (PESE), also referred to as post-exertional malaise (PEM), is defined as the worsening of symptoms that can follow minimal cognitive, physical, emotional, or social activity, or activity that could previously be tolerated. Symptoms typically worsen 12 to 72 hours after activity and can last for days or even weeks, sometimes leading to a relapse.
A congenital malformation with a cleft (gap or opening) in the face.
A neural tube defect characterized by sac-like protrusions of the brain and the membranes that cover it through openings in the skull.
A congenital fistula in the neck resulting from incomplete closure of a branchial cleft.
A general term describing features characterized by abnormal development of bones and connective tissues.
Posterior positions and/or vertical shortening of the infraorbital and perialar regions, or increased concavity of the face and/or reduced nasolabial angle.
A coloboma of the iris.
The presence of calcium- and oxalate-containing calculi (stones) in the kidneys.
A benign nerve sheath tumor composed of Schwann cells.
A tumor of the eye originating from cells of the retina.
An abnormality of the ovary.
The presence of a gonadoblastoma of the ovary.
Abnormally increased hair growth referring to a male pattern of body hair (androgenic hair).
A tumor (abnormal growth of tissue) of the liver.
A reduced desire to eat.
The presence of a neoplasm of the kidney.
A discontinuity of the skin exhibiting complete loss of the epidermis and often portions of the dermis and even subcutaneous fat.
The vomiting of blood.
Severely decreased cardiac output with evidence of inadequate end-organ perfusion (i.e., tissue hypoxia) in the presence of adequate intravascular volume.
An abnormality of the fallopian tube.
A tumor (abnormal growth of tissue) of the ovary.
A cancer of the prostate.
Abnormality of the patella (knee cap).
A type of gait (walking) characterized by by dragging one's feet along or without lifting the feet fully from the ground.
A cyst of the pancreas that possess a lining of mucous epithelium.
An abnormality of the systemic arterial tree, which consists of the aorta and other systemic arteries.
An abnormal reduction in the mobility of ejaculated sperm.
An inflammation of the kidney involving the parenchyma of kidney, the renal pelvis and the kidney calices.
Underdevelopment of the arch of aorta.
Dryness of the mouth due to salivary gland dysfunction.
Difficulty in speaking due to a physical disorder of the mouth, tongue, throat, or vocal cords. Associated with a known physical or neurological cause.
Weakness of the muscles of the arms.
Fasciculations or fibrillation affecting the tongue muscle.
Severe weight loss, wasting of muscle, loss of appetite, and general debility related to a chronic disease.
Bending or curvature of a fifth toe in the tibial direction (i.e., towards the big toe).

An abnormal change (metaplasia) in the cells of the inferior portion of the esophagus. The normal squamous epithelium lining of the esophagus is replaced by metaplastic columnar epithelium. Columnar epithelium refers to a cell type that is typically found in more distal parts of the gastrointestinal system.
An abnormal susceptibility to bleeding, often referred to as a bleeding diathesis. A bleeding diathesis may be related to vascular, platelet and coagulation defects.

Necrosis of the myocardium caused by an obstruction of the blood supply to the heart and often associated with chest pain, shortness of breath, palpitations, and anxiety as well as characteristic EKG findings and elevation of serum markers including creatine kinase-MB fraction and troponin.
Prolongation of the time taken for a standardized skin cut of fixed depth and length to stop bleeding.
An anomaly in platelet form, ultrastructure, or intracellular organelles.
Multiple abnormal growths that arise from the lining of the large intestine (colon or rectum) and protrude into the intestinal lumen.

Polyp-like protrusions which are histologically hamartomas. These can occur throughout the gastrointestinal tract. Hamartomatous polyps are composed of the normal cellular elements of the gastrointestinal tract, but have a markedly distorted architecture.
An abnormality of the prostate.
Abnormal excessive perspiration (sweating) despite the lack of appropriate stimuli like hot and humid weather.

Abnormality of REM Sleep are phases of REM sleep are characterized by desynchronized EEG patterns, increases in heart rate and blood pressure, sympathetic activation, and a profound loss of muscle tone except for the eye and middle-ear muscles. There are also phases of rapid eye movements.

An abnormality of the islet of Langerhans, i.e., of the regions of the pancreas that contain its endocrine cells. These are the alpha cells, which produce glucagon, the beta cells, which produce insulin and amylin, the delta cells, which produce somatostatin, the PP cells, which produce pancreatic polypeptide, and the epsilon cells, which produce ghrelin.
A type of hyperparathyroidism caused by a primary abnormality of the parathyroid glands (e.g., adenoma, carcinoma, hyperplasia). Primary hyperparathyroidism is associated with hyercalcemia.
An increased concentration of insulin in the blood in the fasting state, i.e., not as the response to food intake.
A tumor that originates from a neuroendocrine cell.

A hemangioma is a benign tumor characterized by blood-filled spaces lined by benign endothelial cells. A hemangioma characterized by large endothelial spaces (caverns) is called a cavernous hemangioma (in contrast to a hemangioma with small endothelial spaces, which is called capillary hemangioma).
Localized fluid retention and tissue swelling caused by a compromised lymphatic system.
Neoplasm categorized according to the anatomical site of origin of the neoplasm.
A type of pallor that is secondary to the presence of anemia.
An abnormality of the process of blood coagulation. That is, altered ability or inability of the blood to clot.
An increased concentration of homovanillic acid in the urine.
Abnormal increase in systolic blood pressure.

Abnormally increased weight-to-height squared ratio, calculated by dividing the individual's weight in kilograms by the square of the individual's height in meters and used as an indicator of overweight compared to averages.

A mental disorder characterized by a disintegration of thought processes and emotional responsiveness. It most commonly manifests as auditory hallucinations, paranoid or bizarre delusions, or disorganized speech and thinking. It is accompanied by significant social or occupational dysfunction. The onset of symptoms typically occurs in young adulthood, with a global lifetime prevalence of about 1%. This term is not a helpful parent term to describe abnormal experiences.
Any abnormality of the cardiovascular system.
An abnormally low level of blood oxygen.
An open sore on the surface of the skin of a finger or toe.
A noncongenital process of hair loss, which may progress to partial or complete baldness.
A structural abnormality of the small intestine.
Decreased strength of the muscle layer of stomach, which leads to a decreased ability to empty the contents of the stomach despite the absence of obstruction.
Sparseness of the body hair.
A functional abnormality of the autonomic nervous system.
An abnormality of the upper respiratory tract.
Absence of the eyebrow.
A wartlike (with multiple small elevated projections) papule.
A rupture of the cornea through which a portion of the iris protrudes.
Abnormality/dysplasia of a single myeloid cell (erythroid, granulocytic, or megakaryocytic).
A repeated, painful urge to defecate without excreting stool.
A detrimental reaction to a food, beverage, food additive, or compound found in foods that produces symptoms in one or more body organs and systems that is not mediated by an immune reaction.
Abnormality of glucose homeostasis.
A reduction in the number of corneal endothelial cells.
Hematuria that is visible upon inspection of the urine.

Crackles are discontinuous, explosive, and nonmusical adventitious lung sounds normally heard in inspiration and sometimes during expiration. Crackles are usually classified as fine and coarse crackles based on their duration, loudness, pitch, timing in the respiratory cycle, and relationship to coughing and changing body position.
A darkening of the skin related to an increase in melanin production and deposition.

An exaggerated whealing tendency when the skin is stroked, that is, formation of red, itchy bumps and lines on the skin as a result of pressure on the skin (for instance, stroking the skin with a pen or tongue depressor).
An increased concentration of cholesterol in the blood.
An abnormally increased level of immunoglobulin M in blood.
Greater than normal amounts of fat in the feces. This is a result of malabsorption of lipids in the small intestine and results in frothy foul-smelling fecal matter that floats.
Episodic fever that recurs at regular intervals.

An intermittent atrioventricular block with failure of some atrial impulses to conduct to the ventricles, i.e., some but not all atrial impulses are conducted through the atrioventricular node and trigger ventricular contraction.
An abnormality of the concentration of cortisol in the blood.
An abnormal reduction in the ability to masticate (chew), i.e., in the ability to crush and ground food in preparation for swallowing.
An abnormality of morphology of primary molar.
An abnormal decreased number of leukocytes in the blood.
A decreased concentration of protein in the blood.

Coxa valga is a deformity of the hip in which the angle between the femoral shaft and the femoral neck is increased compared to age-adjusted values (about 150 degrees in newborns gradually reducing to 120-130 degrees in adults).
A decreased ability to move the femur at the hip joint associated with a decreased range of motion of the hip.
Forearm shortening because of underdevelopment of one or more bones of the forearm.
History of repeated intermittent involuntary muscle contractions that were painful.

A sensation of tightness in the neck when attempting to move it, especially after a period of inactivity. Neck stiffness often involves soreness and difficulty moving the neck, especially when trying to turn the head to the side.
The concentration of noradrenaline in the urine, normalized for urine concentration, is above the upper limit of normal.
A cancer of the blood and bone marrow characterized by an abnormal proliferation of leukocytes.
The presence of squamous cell carcinoma of the skin.

A generalized myoclonic seizure is a type of generalized motor seizure characterized by bilateral, sudden, brief (<100 ms) involuntary single or multiple contraction of muscles or muscle groups of variable topography (axial, proximal limb, distal). Myoclonus is less regularly repetitive and less sustained than is clonus.
Atrophy of the cortex of the cerebrum.
An unpleasant sensation characterized by physical discomfort (such as pricking, throbbing, or aching) localized to the eye.
Immunological states where the immune system produces harmful responses upon reexposure to sensitizing antigens.
Increase in periorbital soft tissue.
Persistent abnormal dilatation of the bronchi owing to localized and irreversible destruction and widening of the large airways.
A functional anomaly of the hepatobiliary system
The presence of inflammation of the epididymis.
Testicular inflammation.
Any abnormality of the part of the nervous system that consists of the nerves and ganglia outside of the brain and spinal cord.
Abnormally low glucose concentration in the cerebrospinal fluid.
An abnormality of the urinary bladder.
Increased width of the skull.
The presence of a hernia of the diaphragm present at birth.
A bending or abnormal curvature of the tibia.
A chronic, relapsing, inflammatory, and often febrile multisystemic disorder of connective tissue, characterized principally by involvement of the skin, joints, kidneys, and serosal membranes.
Abnormal accumulation of fluid in the brain.

A contraction of the diaphragm that repeats several times per minute. In humans, the abrupt rush of air into the lungs causes the epiglottis to close, creating a hic sound. Also known as synchronous diaphragmatic flutter (SDF), or singultus, from the Latin singult, the act of catching one's breath while sobbing. The hiccup is an involuntary action involving a reflex arc.

An anomaly of the lymphatic system, a network of lymphatic vessels that carry a clear fluid called lymph unidirectionally towards either the right lymphatic duct or the thoracic duct, which in turn drain into the right and left subclavian veins respectively.
Inflammation of a lymph node.
Severe increase in circulating eosinophils, usually characterized as more than 1500 eosinophils per microlitre.
Acute hepatitis complicated by acute liver failure with hepatic encephalopathy occurring less than 8 weeks after the onset of jaundice.
A deficiency in the intake of energy and nutrients.

Pulmonary hemorrhage is a bleeding within the lungs. Older children and adults may spit blood or bloody sputum. Neonates, infants and young children usually do not spit up blood. Anemia, pulmonary infiltrates, increasingling bloody return on BAL and the presence of hemosiderin-laden macrophages in broncho-alveolar lavage (BAL) fluid or lung biopsy can diagnose lung bleeding. Alveolar macrophages contain phagocytosed red blood cells and stain positive for hemosiderin, a product of hemoglobin degradation, after about 48-72 hours following pulmonary hemorraghe. Previous or recurrent bleeding can thus be distinguished from fresh events. A differentiation into local or diffuse is of importance. Also differentiate if pulmonary hemorrhage is due to a primary lung disorder or a manifestation of a systemic disease.
Bleeding beneath the mucous membrane that lines the inner surface of the eyelid.
Death between the age of 16 and 40 years.
The presence of an adenocarcinoma of the pancreas.
A tumor (abnormal growth of tissue) of the thyroid gland.
Inflammation of the tongue.
An abnormality of the parathyroid gland.
An abnormality of the biliary tree.
Inflammation of the urethra.
Paralysis of the external ocular muscles.
An abnormal accumulation of fluid beneath the skin on the back of the hands.
A neuropathic disorder characterized by episodes of intense pain in the face, originating from the trigeminal nerve. One, two, or all three branches of the nerve may be affected.
Erosion of the mucous mebrane of the mouth with local excavation of the surface, resulting from the sloughing of inflammatory necrotic tissue.
A kind of short stature in which different regions of the body are shortened to a comparable extent.
The presence of circulating autoantibodies to phospholipids.
An increased susceptibility to pneumonia as manifested by a history of recurrent episodes of pneumonia.
A fissure in the gingiva (gums), i.e., the mucosal tissue that lies over the mandible and maxilla.
A non-midline cleft of the upper lip on one side only.
A congenital absence or considerable underdevelopment of the trachea such that communication between the larynx proximally and the alveoli of the lungs distally is lacking.
A defect of development of the brain characterized by congenital absence of the part of the brain that includes the olfactory bulbs, tracts, and other structures associated with the sense of smell.

Anencephaly is a developmental anomaly characterized by a fetus that has no calvarium, with a lack of most or all of the fetus' brain tissue. Anencephaly belongs to a collective group known as neural tube defects (NTD) and is a result of the neural tube failing to close in its rostral end during fetal development.
Onset of disease at the age of between 16 and 40 years.
An inability to digest lactose.
Accumulation of excessive amounts of lymphatic fluid (chyle) in the pleural cavity.
Collapse of part of a lung associated with absence of inflation (air) of that part.

Malignant mesothelioma is a form of cancer that originates from the cells of the mesothelium, a thin tissue layer surrounding the body's internal organs. Malignant mesothelioma is almost exclusively caused by asbestos exposure, pleural mesothelioma being the most common form, affecting the lining of the lungs called the pleura. Other forms such as perioneal-, percardial- or testicular- mesothelioma are much rarer.
The presence of a neoplasm (tumor) in the neurohypophysis, which is also known as the posterior lobe of the hypophysis.
A form of diabetes insipidus related to a failure of vasopressin (AVP) release from the hypothalamus.
A tumor (abnormal growth of tissue) of the thymus.
Any abnormality in the multiplication or reproduction of lymphocytes, which results in the expansion of a cell population.
The presence of autoantibodies (immunoglobulins) in the blood circulation that react against neuromuscular junction acetylcholine receptors.
A tumor (abnormal growth of tissue) of the head and neck region with origin in the lip, oral cavity, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, pharynx, or larynx.

A type of anemia resulting from suppression of erythropoiesis with little or no abnormality of leukocyte or platelet production. Erythroblasts are virtually absent in bone marrow; however, leukocyte and platelet production show little or no reduction.
Stridor is a high pitched sound resulting from turbulent air flow in the upper airway.
A malignant melanoma originating within the eye. The tumor originates from the melanocytes in the uvea (which comprises the iris, ciliary body, and choroid).
Partial displacement of the lens in the inferior direction.
Zonular cataracts are defined to be cataracts that affect specific regions of the lens.
An abnormality affecting one or both hands.
Abnormally increased concentration of cortisol in the urine.
An elevation above normal limits of the concentration of estradiol in the circulation.

A type of atrial arrhythmia characterized by atrial rates of between 240 and 400 beats per minute and some degree of atrioventricular node conduction block. Typically, the ventricular rate is half the atrial rate. In the EKG; atrial flutter waves are observed as sawtooth-like atrial activity. Pathophysiologically, atrial flutter is a form of atrial reentry in which there is a premature electrical impulse creates a self-propagating circuit.

An interatrial communication caused by a deficiency of the common wall between the superior vena cava (SVC) and the right-sided pulmonary veins. SVASD is commonly associated with anomalous pulmonary venous connection (APVC) of some or all of the pulmonary veins, which produces additional left-to-right shunting.
Reduced strength of the musculature of the hand.
Spontaneous pain is a kind of neuropathic pain which occurs without an identifiable trigger.

An arterial lesion that is characterized by either intimal fibroplasia, with neointimal lesions of cells and matrix deposition, or medial fibroplasia, in which there is loss of smooth muscle cells and increased deposition of collagen and proteoglycans in the medial layer.
Presence of a protracted or persistent infection by a pathogen potentially related to an underlying abnormality of the immune system that is not able to clear the infection.
Deposits of various size, shape, consistency, refractive index, and motility within the eye's vitreous humor, which is normally transparent.
Any abnormality in the variability of the time interval between successive heartbeats.
Pneumonia due to the aspiration (breathing in) of food, liquid, or gastric contents into the upper respiratory tract.
Respiratory failure in the newborn.
Reduced function of the gonads (testes in males or ovaries in females) associated with excess pituitary gonadotropin secretion and resulting in delayed sexual development and growth delay.

A reduced level of prolactin in the blood circulation. Prolactin is a protein hormone that is secreted by lactotrophs in the anterior pituitary and that stimulates mammary gland development and milk production.
An avascular or abnormally vascularized retina that occurs in premature infants and can lead to blindness.
Jaundice that is sometimes present, sometimes not.
Small indentation anterior to the insertion of the ear.
An abnormal narrowing of the external auditory canal.
A type of hearing loss resulting from a combination of conductive hearing impairment and sensorineural hearing impairment.
Developmental hypoplasia of the cochlea.
A goiter that is not associated with functional thyroid abnormalities.
Absence of the abdominal musculature.
An abnormality of the uterus.

A localized defect in the bone of the skull resulting from abnormal embryological development. The defect is covered by normal skin. In some cases, skull x-rays have shown underlying lytic bone lesions which have closed before the age of one year.

Short distance from the end of the finger to the most distal interphalangeal crease or the distal interphalangeal joint flexion point. That is, hypoplasia of one or more of the distal phalanx of finger.
Absence or underdevelopment of the toenail.
Disproportionate shortening of the proximal segment of limbs (i.e. the femur and humerus).
An abnormal shortening of the femur.

A hand in which the fingers are of nearly equal length and deflected at the first interphalangeal joint, so as to give a forklike shape consisting of separation of the first and second as well as the third and fourth digits.
An abnormally short femoral neck (which is the process of bone, connecting the femoral head with the femoral shaft).
Parietal bossing is a marked prominence in the parietal region.
Sleep apnea results from a temporary loss of the central drive to the muscles responsible for breathing.
An abnormality of the function of the middle ear.
Enlargement of the anterior fontanelle with respect to age-dependent norms.
An anomaly of the ilium ala. This is the large expanded portion of the ilum which bounds the greater pelvis laterally.
The presence of pigmented, oval and dome-shaped raised hamartomatous nevi of the iris..
Increased sensitivity to stimulation, excluding the special senses, which may refer to various modes of cutaneous sensibility including touch and thermal sensation without pain, as well as to pain.
Abnormal vertical height of the skull and a shortening of its anterior-posterior length, frequently combined with malformations of the occipital region.
Glenoid dysplasia is a developmental anomaly of the scapula that is characterized by a bony deficiency of the posteroinferior glenoid and the adjacent scapular neck.

Infants normally have two fontanels at birth, the diamond-shaped anterior fontanelle at the junction of the coronal and sagittal sutures, and the posterior fontanelle at the intersection of the occipital and parietal bones. The posterior fontanelle usually closes by the 8th week of life, and the anterior fontanel closes by the 18th month of life on average. This term applies if there is delay of closure of the fontanelles beyond the normal age.
Disproportionate shortening of the proximal segment of the arm (i.e. the humerus).

Arnold-Chiari type I malformation refers to a relatively mild degree of herniation of the posteroinferior region of the cerebellum (the cerebellar tonsils) into the cervical canal with little or no displacement of the fourth ventricle. It is characterized by one or both pointed (not rounded) cerebellar tonsils that project 5 mm below the foramen magnum, measured by a line drawn from the basion to the opisthion (McRae Line)
Congenital occlusion of the vagina or adhesion of the walls of the vagina causing occlusion.
Incomplete fusion of the chin, resulting from a developmental defect and manifesting as a midline cleft or fissure of the chin.
Visible increase in width of the non-hallux digit without an increase in the dorso-ventral dimension.

Moderate intellectual disability (ID) is defined as a type of ID characterized by moderately sub-average adaptive functioning and intellectual functioning, with an intelligence quotient (IQ) the range of 35-49.

An intermittent cessation of airflow at the mouth and nose during sleep is known as sleep apnea. Apneas that last at least 10 seconds are considered significant, but individuals with sleep apnea may experience apneas lasting from 20 seconds up to 2 or 3 minutes. Patients may have up to 15 events per hour of sleep.
Developmental hypoplasia (shortening) of middle phalanx of toe.

Tracheal cartilaginous sleeve (TCS) is a rare congenital airway malformation in which distinct tracheal rings are replaced by a continuous cartilaginous segment. Vertically fused C- or O-shaped cartilaginous rings can extend from the subglottis to the carina or bronchus with little to no pars membranacea posteriorly. Comment:Tracheal cartilaginous sleeve has been associated with various craniosynostosis syndromes.
A soft tissue continuity in the anteroposterior axis between the toes 3 and 4.
A form of developmental hypoplasia of the mandible in which the mandible is mislocalised posteriorly.
Hair that is fine or thin to the touch.
Abnormal thickening of the skin localized to the palm of the hand and the sole of the foot.
Elastic fibers in the dermis exhibit an increased number of breaks associated with disorganization of the structure of the elastic fibers.
Meeting of the medial eyebrows in the midline.
Presence of an angular or V -shaped indentation on the ulnar side of the fifth metacarpal bone (i.e., on the sides towards the fifth finger).
Aplasia of frontal sinus.
The absence of a phalangeal segment of a toe or hallux.
Displacement of the 2nd finger towards the radial side.
Synostosis (bony fusion) involving one or more bones of the tarsus (calcaneus, talus, cuboid, navicular, cuneiiform bones).
The distal interphalangeal joint and/or the proximal interphalangeal joint of the fingers cannot be extended to 180 degrees by either active or passive extension.
A developmental defect resulting in the presence of fewer than the normal number of fingers (i.e., aplasia of one or more fingers).
Any structural anomaly of the acrosome resulting in a round sperm head.
A type of lymphoma that originates in B-cells.
Absence of specific immunoglobulins directed against a specific antigen or microorganism.
The presence of thrombocytopenia in combination with detection of antiplatelet antibodies.
Decreased levels of immunoglobulin A (IgA).

Increased susceptibility to opportunistic infections, as manifested by recurrent episodes of infection by opportunistic agents, i.e., by microorganisms that do not usually cause disease in a healthy host, but are able to infect a host with a compromised immune system.
A reduced frequency or duration of eye contact.
A lesser degree of hair pigmentation than would otherwise be expected.
Blockage of the lacrimal duct.
Reduction in thickness of the skin, generally associated with a loss of suppleness and elasticity of the skin.
An abnormality of the development of the toenails.
A developmental defect resulting in abnormal closure, or atresia of the tubular structure of the jejunum.

Missing or malformed long bones of the upper limbs with the distal parts (the hands) connected to the variably shortened or even absent upper extremity, leading to a flipper-like appearance, as opposed to other forms of limb malformations were either the whole limb is missing (such as amelia), or the distal part of a limb is absent (peromelia).

Reduced pigmentation of the fundus, typically generalized. Fundoscopy may reveal a low level pigment in both RPE and choroid with clear visibility of choroidal vessels (pale/albinoid) or low pigment level in the RPE with deep pigment in choroid so that visible choroidal vessels are separated by deeply pigmented zones (tesselated/tigroid).
White color (lack of pigmentation) of the eyebrow.
Formation of abnormal, extraskeletal bony tissue in the soft tissue beneath the skin. Subcutaneous ossifications may be observed by radiography or by palpation.
The presence of calcium deposition in the choroid plexus.
A reduction of bone mineral density, that is, of the amount of matter per cubic centimeter of bones.
Short (hypoplastic) fifth metatarsal bone.
A deviation from the normal concentration of renin in the blood, a central hormone in the control of blood pressure and various other physiological functions.
Redness of the skin of the palm of the hand and the sole of the foot caused by hyperemia of the capillaries in the lower layers of the skin.
The presence of developmental dysplasia of the nail.
A narrow segment of significantly reduced circumference of a digit.
Chronic loss of joint motion in a finger due to structural changes in non-bony tissue.
Protrusion of the meninges through a defect of the skull or vertebral column.
A clearly-defined and roughly linear cleavage in the skin that usually extends to the dermis.
A polar cataract that affects the anterior pole of the lens.
Prominent glomerular basement membrane (GBM), reflecting an increase in thickness (subjective estimate) of the basal lamina of the glomerulus of the kidney.

A degenerative disease of the brain characterized by the insidious onset of dementia. Impairment of memory, judgment, attention span, and problem solving skills are followed by severe apraxia and a global loss of cognitive abilities. The condition primarily occurs after age 60, and is marked pathologically by severe cortical atrophy and the triad of senile plaques, neurofibrillary tangles, and neuropil threads.
Inability to sweat.
Abnormally increased variability in the size of erythrocytes.
An anomaly of erythroid lineage cells, that is, of the erythropoietic cells in the lineage leading to and including erythrocytes.
An anomaly of cellular morphology or physiology.
A type of gait ataxia displaying progression of clinical severity.

A failure to achieve the ability to walk at an appropriate developmental stage. Most children learn to walk in a series of stages, and learn to walk short distances independently between 12 and 15 months.

Atonic seizure is a type of motor seizure characterized by a sudden loss or diminution of muscle tone without apparent preceding myoclonic or tonic event lasting about 1 to 2 seconds, involving head, trunk, jaw, or limb musculature.

Dislocation or malposition of the crystalline lens of the eye. A partial displacement (or dislocation) of the lens is described as a subluxation of the lens, while a complete displacement is termed luxation of the lens. A complete displacement occurs if the lens is completely outside the patellar fossa of the lens, either in the anterior chamber, in the vitreous, or directly on the retina. If the lens is partially displaced but still contained within the lens space, then it is termed subluxation.

Microspherophakia is a rare congenital anomaly characterized by the abnormal spherical shape of the crystalline lens. It is characterized by an increased anteroposterior thickness of the lens associated with reduced equatorial diameter. The primary pathology lies in the development of zonules. The condition is often bilateral and is characterized by small, thick, and spherical lenses.
Transient, non-scarring hair loss and preservation of the hair follicle located in in well-defined patches.
Persistent vaginal dryness.

A developmental disorder of the lacrimal drainage system that most often affects the lacrimal ostium and resulting in non-opening of the nasolacrimal duct. It usually results from a non-canalization of the nasolacrimal duct.
Bilateral absence (atresia) of the posterior nasal aperture (choana).
Pili (from Latin pilus, hair) torti (from Latin tortus, twisted) refers to short and brittle hairs that appear flattened and twisted when viewed through a microscope.
The presence of misshapen or partially destroyed nail plates, often with accumulation of soft, yellow keratin between the dystrophic nail plate and nail bed, resulting in elevation of the nail plate.

Degeneration (wear and tear) of articular cartilage, i.e., of the joint surface. Joint degeneration may be accompanied by osteophytes (bone overgrowth), narrowing of the joint space, regions of sclerosis at the joint surface, or joint deformity.
An abnormal narrowing or constriction of the pulmonary artery, in the main pulmonary artery and/or in the left or right pulmonary artery branches.
An abnormality in which the internal thoraco-abdominal organs demonstrate abnormal arrangement across the left-right axis of the body.
An abnormality of the skin of the palm, that is, the skin of the front of the hand.
Thinned, deficient, or excessively arched ala nasi.
Hypoplasia (congenital reduction in size) of the fifth finger, also known as the little finger.
A condition in which the helix is folded over to a greater degree than normal. That is, excessive curling of the helix edge, whereby the free edge is parallel to the plane of the ear.
Absence of a region of the retina, retinal pigment epithelium, and choroid.
A benign tumor typically found at the junction of the cornea and sclera (limbal epibullar dermoid).
A developmental defect resulting in the congenital absence of skin on the scalp vertex, often just lateral to the midline.
An anomalous configuration of blood vessels that shunts arterial blood directly into veins without passing through the capillaries and that is located in the brain.
Absence of one or more interphalangeal creases (i.e., of the transverse lines in the skin between the phalanges of the fingers).
A persistent midline depression of the skin over the fat pad of the chin.
Spasticity (velocity-dependent increase in tonic stretch reflexes with increased muscle tone and hyperexcitable tendon reflexes) in the muscles of the lower limbs, hips, and pelvis.

Spasticity is manifested by increased stretch reflex which is intensified with movement velocity. This results in excessive and inappropriate muscle activation which can contribute to muscle hypertonia. Spastic gait is characterized by manifestations such as muscle hypertonia, stiff knee, and circumduction of the leg.
Presence of only 11 pairs of ribs.
Dislocation of the distal humerus out of the elbow joint, where the radius, ulna, and humerus meet.
An abnormal conformation of the femur that becomes gradually enlarged towards the proximal end. This feature affects the proximal femoral metaphysis and epiphysis.

The rib cage has the shape of a wide mouthed bell. That is, the superior portion of the rib cage is constricted, followed by a convex region, and the inferior portion of the rib cage expands again to have a large diameter.
Absence or underdevelopment of the ulna.
Reduced width of the chest from side to side, associated with a reduced distance from the sternal notch to the tip of the shoulder.

An abnormal hand posture in which the hands are clenched to fists. All digits held completely flexed at the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints. In prenatal sonography of the fetal clenched hand, the index finger overlaps a clenched fist formed by the other digits. The proximal interphalangeal articulation of the index finger is flexed and ulnarly deviated, and the thumb is adducted.
The presence of abnormal punctate (speckled, dot-like) calcifications in the humeral epiphysis.
Underdevelopment (reduced size) of the tibia.
Diffuse thickening of the ventricular endocardium and by associated myocardial dysfunction
Any complex of structural, architectural, contractile or electrophysiological changes affecting the atria with the potential to produce clinically relevant manifestations.
A rare congenital vascular anomaly that results when the left superior cardinal vein caudal to the innominate vein fails to regress.
Absence or underdevelopment of the ear lobes.
Abnormality of the wrist, the structure connecting the hand and the forearm.

The clinical electro-oculogram (EOG) is an electrophysiological test of function of the outer retina and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) in which changes in electrical potential across the RPE are recorded during successive periods of dark and light adaptation.
Fasciculations affecting the tongue muscle and the musculature of the face.
Truncal ataxia is a sign of ataxia characterized by instability of the trunk. It usually occurs during sitting.
A vertical gaze palsy with inability to direct the gaze of the eyes downwards.
Absence of the Achilles reflex (also known as the ankle jerk reflex), which can normally be elicited by tapping the tendon is tapped while the foot is dorsiflexed.
Inflammation of the esophagus.
An abnormality of the neck.
A bifid rib refers to cleavage of the sternal end of a rib, usually unilateral. Bifid ribs are usually asymptomatic, and are often discovered incidentally by chest x-ray.
Complete or partial merging of adjacent ribs.
A developmental defect leading to the union of two adjacent vertebrae.
A fibroma of the heart.
Recurrent episodes of ulceration of the oral mucosa, typically presenting as painful, sharply circumscribed fibrin-covered mucosal defects with a hyperemic border.
Edema in the region of the upper eyelid.
Sustained involuntary muscle contractions that produce twisting and repetitive movements of the body.
Abnormality of tear production.
Decreased density/number and/or decreased diameter of lateral eyebrow hairs.
Presenile cataract is a kind of cataract that occurs in early adulthood, that is, at an age that is younger than usual.
An increased tendency to fractures of the long bones (Mainly, the femur, tibia, fibula, humerus, radius, and ulna).
Longitudinal densities on radiographs located in a metaphysis (the narrow region of a long bone between the epiphysis and the diaphysis).
A neoplasm containing histiocytes.
Underdevelopment of the nasal septum.
An abnormality of the formation and mineralization of one or more vertebrae.
An abnormally small sella turcica.
An abnormal anterior bending or curvature of the tibia.

Radial dysplasia, also known as radial longitudinal deficiency, includes radial clubhand and is a disfiguring, and potentially disabling, congenital limb anomaly. The entire upper limb may be involved, although the defect is most evident in the forearm and hand. Affected children suffer a variable degree of hypoplasia or absence of the preaxial skeleton and soft tissues, in particular the thumb, radius, and dorsoradial soft tissues. The hand is usually radially deviated and subluxated off the distal aspect of the ulna, the ulna may be shortened and have a bow-shaped deformity, and there is no true wrist (radiocarpal) joint in Bayne2 type-III and IV radial dysplasia.
Abnormally flat shape of the heads of the metatarsal bones.
Displacement of the 3rd finger towards the radial side (i.e., towards the thumb).
Increased side-to-side width of the metacarpal epiphyses.

For children from birth to 4 years of age the palm width is more than 2 SD above the mean; for children from 4 to 16 years of age the palm width is above the 95th centile; or, the width of the palm appears disproportionately wide for the length.
Medial deviation of the second toe.
A developmental defect characterized by undergrowth of the sacrum, which is a large, triangular bone at the base of the spine that forms by the fusing of the sacral vertebrae (S1-S5).
Contractures of one ore more joints of the hands meaning chronic loss of joint motion due to structural changes in non-bony tissue.
Absence or underdevelopment of the distal phalanges.
An increase in width of the distal phalanx of the big toe.
This type of brachydactyly is characterized by short and broad terminal phalanges of the thumbs and big toes.
An abnormal shape or form of the proximal phalanx of the big toe.
An abnormality of the morphology of the toes, such that the tips of the toes are prominent and bulbous.
Any structural anomaly of the mitral valve.
The palpebral fissure inclination is more than two standard deviations above the mean for age (objective); or, the inclination of the palpebral fissure is greater than typical for age.
Depression located on the vermilion of the lower lip, usually paramedian.
Sex limitation is used to refer to a monogenic trait linked to an autosomal locus in which the phenotypic effects of allelic differences are expressed only in one sex.
A structural lymph node abnormality.
The formation of new bone along the cortex and underneath the periosteum of a bone.
Abnormally increased thickness of the cortical layer of the ulna.
Thickening of the periosteum of long bone.
The presence of a vaginal septum, thereby creating a vaginal duplication. The septum is longitudinal in the majority of cases.
A partial dislocation of a joint.
Distance between the medial and lateral canthi is more than 2 SD below the mean for age (objective); or, apparently reduced length of the palpebral fissures.
A moderate delay in the achievement of motor or mental milestones in the domains of development of a child.
Underdevelopment of the ilium ala.
Onset prior to birth.

Describes a foot digit resting on the dorsal surface of an adjacent digit when the foot is at rest. Initially clawing may be dynamic and only noticeable on walking. Over time the plantar plate tears, subluxation occurs at the metatarsophalangeal joint (MTPJ), and the deformity becomes permanent.
Low set, steeply sloping shoulders.
A confluent, generalized overgrowth of silvery blonde to gray lanugo hair at birth.
Unusual prominence of the median palatal raphe, which is the ridge formed by the fusion of the two plates of the skull that form the hard palate.
Excessive, increased hair growth located in the sacral region.

Systemic desaturation of a liveborn baby resulting from persistent pulmonary hypertension with a patent ductus arteriosus and patent foramen ovale, such that the circulation in postnatal life follows the fetal course.

The trabecular septum is the largest part of the interventricular septum. It extends from the membranous septum to the apex and superiorly to the infundibular septum. A defect in the trabecular septum is called muscular VSD if the defect is completely rimmed by muscle.

Inability of the left ventricle to perform its normal physiologic function. Failure is either due to an inability to contract the left ventricle or the inability to relax completely and fill with blood during diastole.
Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) is an abnormally increased heart rate (over 100 beats per minute at rest) with origin above the level of the ventricles.
Right ventricular dysfunction (global or regional) with functional and morphological right ventricular abnormalities, with or without left ventricular disease.
Loss of hair in the occipital region of the scalp with congenital onset.
Pheochromocytoma originating from the adrenal medulla.
The presence of a fistula affecting the rectum.
An abnormal site of the kidney.
A type of congenital cataract in which the opacity follows the anterior or posterior Y suture.
A collection of pus in the area of the rectum.
Increased susceptibility to staphylococcal infections, as manifested by recurrent episodes of staphylococcal infections.
Increased susceptibility to fatigue.
Any deviation from the normal circulating creatine kinase concentration.
A bilateral tonic-clonic seizure with focal onset is a focal-onset seizure which progresses into a bilateral tonic-clonic phase.

A type of kinetic tremor that occurs during target directed movement is called intention tremor. That is, an oscillatory cerebellar ataxia that tends to be absent when the limbs are inactive and during the first part of voluntary movement but worsening as the movement continues and greater precision is required (e.g., in touching a target such as the patient's nose or a physician's finger).
Maxillary teeth cover the mandibular teeth when biting to an increased degree. The feature is defined as a vertical overlap of the maxillary incisors over the mandibular incisors that exceeds 2 mm.
An abnormality of eye movement characterized by impaired smooth-pursuit eye movements.
A type of dysmetria involving the limbs.
Protruding heel bone, or calcaneus.

A failure to achieve the ability to crawl at an appropriate developmental stage. Normal infant motor development is marked by a series of postural milestones including learning to crawl on hands and knees between the ages of 6 and 10 months.
A manifest or latent ocular deviation in which one or both eyes tends to deviate nasally.
A manifest or latent ocular deviation in which one or both eyes tends to deviate temporally.
Two-sided or bilateral weakness of the muscles of facial expression and eye closure.
Muscular hypotonia (abnormally low muscle tone) manifesting in the neonatal period and affecting the entire musculature.
A deficit in the ability to fixate eye movements in order to stabilize images on the retina
Any abnormality of bones of the arms or legs.
Involuntary movements of one hand that accompany and mirror intentional movements of the opposite hand.
Defective structure and function of myelin sheaths. Dysmyelination is distinguished from demyleination where there is destruction or damage of previously normal myelination.
A reduction in the number of axons in the peripheral nervous system.
Weakness of the peroneal muscles.
A congenital deformity characterized by a dorsiflexed, inverted, and adducted foot, i.e., a combination of talipes calcaneus and talipes varus.
Bigonial distance (lower facial width) more than 2 SD above the mean (objective); or an apparently increased width of the lower jaw (mandible) when viewed from the front (subjective).
Abnormality of the eleventh cranial nerve.
The presence of reduced numbers of intrahepatic bile duct than normal.
A reduction of joint mobility resulting from changes involving the articular surfaces.
Undergrowth of the outer labia.
A pterygium (or pterygia) occurring in the popliteal region (the back of the knee).
An abnormal amount of hair.

Euryblepharon is a congenital eyelid anomaly characterized by horizontal enlargement of the palpebral fissure. The eyelid is shortened vertically compared with the horizontal dimension, with associated lateral canthal malpositioning and lateral ectropion abnormally wide lid opening.
Increased range of shoulder movement related to aplasia or hypoplasia of the clavicles that results in the ability to approximate the shoulders in front of the chest.
Delayed tooth eruption affecting the primary dentition.
Underdevelopment of frontal sinus.

A cone-shaped appearance of the epiphyses of the fingers of the hand, producing a 'ball-in-a-socket' appearance. The related entity 'angel-shaped' epiphysis refers to a pronounced cone-shaped epiphysis in combination with a pseudoepiphysis at the distal end of a phalanx.
Complete bilateral fractures of the pars interarticularis resulting in the anterior slippage of the vertebra.
Absence of the tibia.
A congenital disorder of the aortic valve in which the orifice of the valve fails to develop.
An abnormality of the normal developmental rotation of the kidney leading to an abnormal orientation of the kidney.
A cleft of the optic nerve that extends inferiorly.
A chronic loss of wrist joint motion due to structural changes in muscle, tendons, ligaments, or skin that prevent normal movement of the joints of the wrist.
One or more flexion contractures (a bent joint that cannot be straightened actively or passively) that are present at birth.
A reduced concentration of copper in the blood.
Congenital absence or underdevelopment of the fovea centralis.
Abnormal relative increase in the amount of fecal coproporphyrin III as compared to coproporphyrin I in the feces.
Inability to move the muscles of respiration.

The presence of fine, branching linear opacities in Bowman's layer in the central area that may spread to the periphery in the clinical course. The deep corneal stroma may be involved but the process does not reach Descemet's membrane. Recurrent corneal erosion may occur. Histologic examination reveals amyloid deposits in the collagen fibers of the cornea.
Reduced transparency of the central posterior portion of the corneal stroma.
A type of astigmatism in which the principle meridians are not 90 degrees apart and which is associated with loss of vision.
Atrophy of the capillary lamina of choroid.
An unpleasant sensation characterized by physical discomfort (such as pricking, throbbing, or aching) localized to the lower back.
An exostosis is a benign growth the projects outward from the bone surface. It is capped by cartilage, and arises from a bone that develops from cartilage.
Increased side-to-side width of the first metatarsal bone.
A progressive degree of muscular rigidity (continuous contraction of muscles with constant resistance to passive movement).
Unilateral paresis (weakness) with spasticity of the affected muscles and increased tendon reflexes.

Lack of visual responsiveness or decrease in visual capabilities suggesting a lack of visual responsiveness or decrease in visual capabilities in an infant or young child in which visual behavior fails to meet normal developmental milestones.
Nystagmus due to disturbance of the vestibular system; eye movements are rhythmic, with slow and fast components.
The presence of amyloid deposition in the nerves of the peripheral nervous system.
A form of hypersociability that presents as mostly inappropriate friendliness towards others.

An enduring pattern of uncooperative, defiant, and hostile behavior towards authority figures that does not involve major antisocial violations, is not accounted for by the child's developmental stage, and results in significant functional impairment. A certain level of oppositional behavior is common in children and adolescents.
Increased level of cryoglobulins in the blood. Cryoglobulins are abnormal immunoglobulins, especially IGG or IGM, that precipitate spontaneously when serum is cooled below 37 degrees Celsius.

Cryptophthalmos is a condition of total absence of eyelids and the skin of forehead is continuous with that of cheek, in which the eyeball is completely concealed by the skin, which is stretched over the orbital cavity.
Skin crease extending from below the inner canthus laterally along the malar process of the maxilla and zygoma.

Disseminated multifocal hemangiomatous or lymphangiomatous lesions of the skeleton. The lesions are lytic, well-defined, round or oval lesions within the medullary cavity, and they have an intact cortex, and manifest variable peripheral sclerosis and may exhibit endosteal scalloping.
An unpleasant sensation characterized by physical discomfort (such as pricking, throbbing, or aching) localized to the mandible.
Bipolar disorder is an illness of mood characterized by alternating episodes of elevated and depressed moods, which are interspersed with euthymic periods.
Absence of nail of little finger.
Ophthalmoplegia is a paralysis or weakness of one or more of the muscles that control eye movement.
Radiolucency (reflecting a reduction in the bony substance) around the apex (the tip of the dental root).
Developmental dysplasia of dentin affecting only the primary dentition.
Raised, well-circumscribed areas of erythema and edema involving the dermis and epidermis. Urticaria is intensely pruritic, and blanches completely with pressure.

A state of excessive water intake and hypotonic (dilute) polyuria. Diabetes insipidus may be due to failure of vasopressin (AVP) release (central or neurogenic diabetes insipidus) or to a failure of the kidney to respond to AVP (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus).

Retinal dystrophy is an abnormality of the retina associated with a hereditary process. Retinal dystrophies are defined by their predominantly monogenic inheritance and they are frequently associated with loss or dysfunction of photoreceptor cells as a primary or secondary event.
Well-demarcated area(s) of partial or complete depigmentation in the macula, reflecting atrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium with associated retinal photoreceptor loss.

A type of retinal detachment arising from damage to the outer blood-retinal barrier that allows fluid to access the subretinal space and separate the neurosensory retina from the retinal pigment epithelium.
Underdevelopment of the optic disc, that is of the optic nerve head, where ganglion cell axons exit the eye to form the optic nerve.
Underdevelopment of the stroma of iris.
Underdevelopment of the ischium, which forms the lower and back part of the hip bone.
Underdevelopment of the bony pelvis.
Persistence of the primary teeth beyond the age by which they normally are shed and replaced by the permanent teeth.

An anomaly related to partial closure, or failure of development of the ulnar side of the distal radial growth plate, which results in an arrest of epiphyseal growth of the medial and volar portions of the distal radius. This leads to shortening of the radius and relative overgrowth of the ulna.
Decreased amount of pigmentation in the macula lutea.
A body habitus that is tall, slim and underweight, with long legs and long arms (i.e., arm span exceeds height by 5 cm or more).
A deficit in coordination of mulscle movements. Coordination is defined as the orchestrated movement of multiple body parts as required to accomplish intended actions, like walking.
A decrease in the ability to perceive vibration in the distal portions of the limbs.
A reduced degree of motion of the muscles beneath the skin of the face, often associated with reduced facial crease formation.
An abnormality of the malleus, an ossicle in the middle ear.
A bilateral type of conductive hearing impairment.

Decreased ratio between the upper and the lower segment of the body, where the lower segment is defined as the length between the top of pubic symphysis to floor, and the upper segment is defined as the top of head to top of pubic symphysis. Consider the term Disproportionate tall stature (HP:0001519) if tall stature is also present.
A type of hyperbilirubinemia with neonatal onset.
A structural anomaly of the nasopharynx.
A type of holoprosencephaly in which the left and right frontal and parietal lobes are fused and the interhemispheric fissure is only present posteriorly.
The presence of a hernia in which the upper part of the stomach, i.e., mainly the gastric cardia protrudes through the diaphragmatic esophageal hiatus.
A displacement or misalignment of the humerus with respect to the other bones of the should joint. Note that a subluxation is a partial dislocation.
Loss of elasticity of the upper and lower eyelids causing the skin to sag and bulge.
Weakness in the supporting structures of the pelvic floor allowing the pelvic viscera to descend or one or more of the pelvic organs drop from their normal position.

Pulmonary bullae are rounded focal regions of emphysema with a thin wall which measure more than 1 cm in diameter. They are often subpleural in location and are typically larger in the apices. In some cases, bullae can be very large and result in compression of adjacent lung tissue. A giant bulla is arbitrarily defined as one that occupies at least one third of the volume of a hemithorax.
